 The best laptop power banks are a must-buy when you're working away from a power socket. After all, even the best laptops for photo editing won't run on battery forever. And with governments telling us all to stock up on food and prepare for power outages, a power bank is a great way of ensuring you can keep vital devices going for a few days if the mains electricity fails to flow.
 But, the best iPhone power banks won't be powerful enough to do the job. Instead, you'll need a power bank with at least 18,000mAh capacity, as well as the right ports to connect to your specific laptop.
 As an added bonus, with a power bank this powerful, you'll be able to charge your cameras, tablets, phones,and other devices too. To find you the best model for your needs, we've put our experts to work. They've been testing and reviewing power banks, as well as using them within their own workflows, in order to compile this list of the absolute best.

And knowing exactly how fast my laptop is charging is both just plain interesting to know, but I can also plan ahead to give make sure I have enough juice left throughout the day.
 The Anker Prime power isn’t just about a screen though, it also has a solid 20,000mAh of battery which I managed to get a few days' worth of keeping my phone and laptop going with short bursts of recharging, or one big recharge of my MacBook Pro 13. The big 200W maximum output, with a 100W single port output, also allowed me to use my laptop at full power. The power bank is a little boxy for slipping into pockets, but it looks great.

 Will one of the best portable chargers work for a laptop?
 Sadly not, you will need a power bank with a much higher capacity than most power banks used to charge camera phones or other small appliances. It's recommended that you invest in a power bank with a 20,000 mAh or larger especially if you want to charge it multiple times. 
 How do I connect my laptop to the powerbank?
 How you connect your laptop to your power bank will depend on the time of charging cable your laptop needs. While most modern laptops such as the Apple Macbook Pro 14 M2 will have a USB C input, some older models might still use round AC adapters or a standard USB A input. For a thin ultrabook that usually means 65W, and the INIU 20,000mAh 65W is our pick. For a 14-inch laptop, 100W is safer, and for a MacBook Pro class laptop you want 140W, which the Anker Prime 300W gives.

 How to match a power bank to your laptop 
 Look at the charger that came with your laptop. The label says how many watts it delivers. A power bank needs to deliver about the same on a single USB-C port. A bank with less will still charge the laptop, but slowly, and it may not keep up while you work.

 Remember that the number on the box is often total output. What matters for a laptop is the maximum on a single USB-C port.

 How to choose a power bank for a laptop 
 1. Start with your charger’s watts
 Match or beat the number on your charger. If you are unsure, go one step up.
 2. Check the single-port output
 A bank may advertise 300W but only give 140W on one port. Your laptop uses one port.
 3. Use a good USB-C cable
 For 100W and above, use a cable rated for it. A cheap cable can limit the power.
 4. Mind the weight
 Laptop banks weigh 13 to 21 ounces. The weight chart above shows the range.
 5. Think about flying
 Airlines limit power banks to 100 Wh in carry-on bags. All five here are under it. Never pack one in checked luggage.
 6. Check the warranty
 The INIU and JUOVI give 3 years. The Anker banks give 18 to 24 months. The UGREEN did not show a length.

 Can a power bank charge a laptop? 
 Yes, if it has a USB-C Power Delivery port with enough watts and your laptop charges over USB-C. Many newer laptops do. Check your laptop’s charger label.
 How many watts does a power bank need to charge a laptop? 
 About the same as your laptop’s own charger. Thin laptops often need 45W to 65W, 14-inch laptops 65W to 100W and 16-inch laptops 100W to 140W.
 Will a 65W power bank charge a 100W laptop? 
 It may charge slowly, and may not keep up while you work. For best results, match the power of the original charger.
 Can I take a laptop power bank on a plane? 
 Yes in carry-on, if it is under 100 Wh. All five banks here are under that. Never pack a power bank in checked luggage.
 How long will a power bank run my laptop? 
 It depends on the laptop and what you do. A 20,000mAh bank gives roughly 0.9 of a 60 Wh laptop charge. The larger banks give a bit over one.
 Do I need a special cable? 
 For 100W and above, yes. Use a cable rated for the power you need. A cheap cable can limit charging.

 The Rapid Pro offers a laundry list of charging capabilities (PD3.1, PPS, QC3.0, AFC, Apple2.4A, BC1.2, SCP, FCP, UFCS), but its greatest feature could be its super speedy recharge rate. Charge from a single USB-C input at 140 watts, and it takes an hour or so to fill, but you can plug in both at once to hit 80 percent from dead in under half an hour. Even better, Ecoflow’s dock can charge via the pogo pins on the bottom at 320 watts, enabling you to go from zero to 80 percent in just 20 minutes. You can fully charge it while you pack a bag. It looks cool, with a smart display showing battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts, and it supports Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, among other standards.  Photograph: Simon Hill 
 Anker 737 Power Bank for $110 : This is a versatile and reliable 24,000-mAh-capacity power bank that supports power delivery 3.1 and can send or receive up to 140 watts to charge laptops. You can charge it from zero within an hour. It’s relatively compact, but it weighs almost 1.4 pounds. The snazzy digital display shows the remaining battery percentage and stats, including the temperature, total output, cycles, and more. It fast-charged everything I tested it with, and you can charge three devices at once without a problem.
 Ugreen 145W Power Bank for $65 : Surprisingly compact for a 25,000-mAh battery, this weighs 1.1 pounds and has two USB-C ports and one USB-A port. Our former pick for tablets, the Ugreen, actually offers 145 watts, one USB-C port at 100W, and the other at 45W. There's a small LED readout on the side of the battery with the current charge state of the battery. I'd have liked to see some charging info on that screen as well, but that's a small quibble with what's an otherwise outstanding option if you need to keep your tablet or iPad charged up wherever you are.
 Cuktech 15 Ultra for $79: With impressive build quality, including a nice grippy material on the underside and a handy display showing power output and input, this Cuktech (pronounced chook-tek) power bank boasts 20,000-mAh capacity, can charge two or three devices simultaneously at up to 165 watts, and supports many fast-charging protocols including PPS, QC, PD3.1, FCP, SCP, and MiPPS.
 Laptop Power Bank FAQ
 What Features Should I Look for in a Power Bank?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.
 The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get out depends on the cable you use , the device you're charging, and the charging method (Qi wireless charging is less efficient). You will never get the maximum capacity. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for a laptop battery.
 The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. For best results match the charging speed across the power bank, cable, and laptop.
 Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. Many portable chargers support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.
 Can I Take a Power Bank on a Flight?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 It’s safe to fly with a power bank , but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours (WH). If your power bank has a capacity larger than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.
 Some airlines have introduced stricter rules, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have onboard.
 How I Test Power Banks
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 I've been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test laptop (currently a MacBook Air). I'll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL, iPhone 16, and whatever else I have in. For this guide, I also tested with a Chromebook. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.
 Aside from standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it's not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.
 How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 I scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to these companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would be against WIRED's editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision process when ranking.
 There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to reputable brands, but there's always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

Best Power Bank for Laptop: 140W and 100Wh Picks | ComputingForGeeks 
 Skip to content 
 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 The best power bank for laptop travel clears two bars. Its USB-C port matches your laptop charger’s watts, and its rating stays under 100 Wh so it boards the plane with you. That second bar got stricter this year. Since 27 March 2026, ICAO rules cap you at two power banks in the cabin. IATA also says airline approval for 100 to 160 Wh power banks ends with its 1 January 2027 rules, so anything bigger is a bad buy for a flyer.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 178503 
 You get six picks for a big laptop, a travel router running Tailscale or WireGuard , a Raspberry Pi 5 and a mini PC, plus how to read PD wattage and PPS. None of these banks went through our lab; capacity figures come from independent discharge tests. We checked specs against maker pages, prices through Amazon’s API and airline rules against IATA, FAA and airline notices in October 2026.
 Pick a laptop power bank at a glance
 Every bank on this list rates under 100 Wh, so all six fit the no-approval cabin tier. Two of them (the Anker 737 and the INIU) don’t print the Wh figure on their maker pages, so read the label on the bank itself. What separates them is how many watts one USB-C port can deliver and what else you need to run from it:
 Best overall for a 16-inch laptop: Anker Prime 26K 300W (A110A). Two USB-C ports at 140 W each, 99.75 Wh, and a display that shows watts per port. Check the price on Amazon .
 Best value for two laptops: EcoFlow RAPID Pro 27,650mAh 300W. Two 140 W ports, one of them a built-in retractable cable, at 99.54 Wh. Check the price on Amazon .
 Best for a USB-C mini PC: Anker 737 (PowerCore 24K, A1289). 140 W from one USB-C port (70 W each when two share it), with independently measured capacity. Check the price on Amazon .
 Best budget 140 W: UGREEN Nexode 25000mAh 145W. A 140 W port for well under $100, with a slow 65 W refill. Check the price on Amazon .
 Best for a travel router and phone: INIU 20000mAh 65W (P62-E1). Small, 324 g, with PPS listed and enough for a 13-inch ultrabook. Check the price on Amazon .
 Best for 12 V barrel-jack gear: Talentcell PB030201-35. A 12 V DC output next to a 45 W USB-C port, at 76.65 Wh. Check the price on Amazon .
 If your 13 or 14-inch laptop ships with a 65 W charger, you do not need a 140 W bank. The INIU covers it at about half the weight of the big Ankers, and the money you save buys a better travel router.
 See how we picked
 We started from what a laptop, a router and a mini PC ask a USB-C port for. Then we pulled the Amazon US catalog through the Creators API on 27 October 2026. A bank made the list only if it passed all of these:
 Its capacity works out under 100 Wh, from the maker’s Wh figure or from its mAh rating where the maker prints only that, so it boards without airline approval.
 You get at least one USB-C port that matches a common laptop charger: 65 W, 100 W or 140 W.
 You can buy it new from Amazon US today, and the listing matches the model on the maker page.
 You aren’t buying a model named in a 2025 or 2026 power bank recall that our search of recall news turned up.
 We did not bench these banks ourselves, so every capacity number below names its source. TechRadar measured the Anker 737 with a ChargerLAB POWER-Z meter, and techtest.org ran discharge tests on the Anker Prime 26K and the 737.
 Two popular banks missed the cut. We could not confirm the Baseus Blade 100W’s Wh rating or weight on a Baseus page. The CUKTECH 20 rates well at techtest.org, but its maker page would not load for us.
 Compare the power bank specs side by side
 The Wh column is the one that matters at the airport, and the single-port column is the one that matters to your laptop. Prices are Amazon US on 27 October 2026 and they move every week:
 Power bank Printed rating Best single USB-C port PPS Recharge input Weight Price 
 Anker Prime 26K 300W 26,250 mAh, 99.75 Wh 140 W (28 V 5 A), on both C ports Not listed by Anker; measured by techtest.org 140 W per port, 250 W with both 600 g about $200 
 EcoFlow RAPID Pro 27,650mAh 27,650 mAh, 99.54 Wh 140 W, on two of four C outputs Not listed 280 W 699 g about $110 on sale ($176 list) 
 Anker 737 (24K) 24,000 mAh, 86.4 Wh (per TechRadar) 140 W (28 V 5 A) Measured by techtest.org 140 W (28 V 5 A) about 630 g about $110 
 UGREEN Nexode 25000mAh 145W 25,000 mAh, 90 Wh 140 W on C1, 65 W on C2 No 65 W 513 g about $80 
 INIU 20000mAh 65W 20,000 mAh, Wh not printed online 65 W (20 V 3.25 A) Listed, range unpublished 45 W 324 g about $42 
 Talentcell PB030201-35 76.65 Wh 45 W, plus 12 V DC out Not listed 12.6 V barrel charger Not published about $50 
 The first two rows show why mAh is the wrong number to shop by. The EcoFlow lists 1,400 mAh more than the Anker Prime, yet the Anker prints the higher Wh figure. The arithmetic implies Anker counts its cells at about 3.8 V and EcoFlow at about 3.6 V. Wh is what a bank stores and what airline staff read off the label, so compare that column and ignore the mAh race.
 The “300W” and “145W” in the product names are totals across every port. They are not what one laptop gets.
 Get the Anker Prime 26K 300W for a 16-inch laptop
 This is the bank to buy if your laptop came with a 140 W USB-C charger and you want it to charge from the bank at the same speed. Both USB-C ports do 140 W at 28 V and 5 A, so you can plug a big laptop into either one without checking which port is the fast one.
 Anker Prime 26K 300W (A110A): 99.75 Wh with two 140 W USB-C ports. Image: Anker. 
 Who it suits: you travel with a 16-inch laptop, often carry a second device that wants fast charging too, and you’d rather read the watts on a screen than guess. Look elsewhere if you mostly charge a 65 W ultrabook, because you’d be carrying 600 g and paying about $200 for headroom you never use.
 Anker rates the A110A at 26,250 mAh and 99.75 Wh, just under the 100 Wh cabin line. It has two USB-C ports at up to 140 W each, a 22.5 W USB-A port and a 300 W combined ceiling. It refills at 140 W through one port or 250 W through both.
 Expert Reviews ran 140 W, 140 W and 20 W at once. techtest.org found it held 140 W steadily and treated 300 W as a short peak that throttles back. It measured 79.6 to 89.8 Wh delivered, about 80 to 90 percent of the label. That is a normal loss for boosting cell voltage up to 20 or 28 V.
 The one gap is PPS. Anker’s own pages do not list it for the A110A, although techtest.org’s unit offered PPS from 4.5 to 21 V at up to 5 A. That test is encouraging if your phone needs PPS, but it is not a spec Anker promises.
 A 240 W cable and a 24-month warranty come with it. The bundle with a charging base costs about $80 more, and you don’t need the base. It sells for about $200, so check the live price before you buy.
 Save with the EcoFlow RAPID Pro for two laptops
 The EcoFlow RAPID Pro matches the Anker Prime on the numbers that count: two 140 W outputs and a rating just under 100 Wh. On 27 October 2026 it sold for about $90 less. If you charge two laptops at once, it’s the better buy at that price.
 EcoFlow RAPID Pro 27,650mAh 300W: 99.54 Wh, two 140 W outputs and two 65 W ports. Image: EcoFlow. 
 Buy it if you share a bank between two laptops, or you lose cables and want one that can’t be left behind. Look elsewhere if weight matters most. At 699 g it is the heaviest bank here, and a built-in cable is one more part that wears out.
 EcoFlow lists 27,650 mAh, a 140 W single-port maximum and a 300 W multi-port total. Macworld gave it an Editors’ Choice and lists 99.54 Wh. Its two 140 W PD 3.1 outputs include a 60 cm retractable cable, and two 65 W USB-C ports sit beside them. Macworld confirmed both 140 W outputs work at the same time.
 The bank refills at up to 280 W over USB-C. EcoFlow’s 320 W figure needs its own desktop charger or pogo-pin dock, so plan on the USB-C number.
 A “RAPID Pro X” listing at about $190 is a different product we did not verify, so make sure your cart holds the 27,650mAh 300W model. It sells for about $110 on sale against a $176 list price, so check the live price before you buy.
 Run a USB-C mini PC on the Anker 737
 The Anker 737 is the bank we’d hand a mini PC or a 140 W laptop when one device gets all the power. It has been on sale since 2022, and that is the point. More than one reviewer has measured its capacity, and the numbers agree.
 Anker 737 (A1289): 24,000 mAh and a single 140 W USB-C port. Image: Anker. 
 It fits you when you run one hungry device at a time, like a USB-C mini PC with no outlet nearby, and you want known runtime numbers. Look elsewhere if you need two fast ports. The 737 splits to 70 W and 70 W once a second USB-C device plugs in.
 The 737 has two USB-C ports and one USB-A, a 140 W ceiling at 28 V and 5 A, and a 140 W recharge input. TechRadar lists it at 86.4 Wh. It measured 77.1 Wh delivered at 20 V and 5 A (89 percent), and 73.1 Wh at 28 V. techtest.org’s 2026 unit averaged 74.63 Wh across its loads and offered PPS from 4.5 to 21 V.
 Pass-through charging runs up to 90 W. TechRadar notes the bank does not refill itself while doing it and has no UPS mode, so do not use it as backup for a mini PC that must never drop power. A power station or a real UPS does that job.
 Anker’s pages disagree on weight (607 g and 630 g), and techtest.org weighed 641 g, so plan on about 630 g. Early 2022 units had a 28 V problem with the Framework Laptop 16, which techtest.org did not see on its 2026 unit. It sells for about $110, so check the live price before you buy.
 Spend less with the UGREEN Nexode 145W
 This UGREEN gets you a 140 W USB-C port for about $80, the cheapest route to full-speed charging on a 140 W laptop in this guide. The savings come out of the refill speed and the second port.
 UGREEN Nexode 25000mAh 145W: 90 Wh, 140 W on one USB-C port. Image: UGREEN. 
 Good match: you want one big laptop charged fast on a budget, and you can top the bank up overnight. Look elsewhere if you refill between flights or your phone needs PPS. This bank lists neither a fast refill nor PPS.
 UGREEN’s spec table for SKU 90597A lists 25,000 mAh at 3.6 V (90 Wh). You get 140 W on C1, 65 W on C2 and 22.5 W on USB-A, with 145 W as the combined total. Only C1 accepts input, and only at 65 W. That is less than half the Ankers’ refill speed, so a bank you drain on the plane takes far longer to fill at the hotel. The protocol list covers PD 3.0 and QC 3.0 but not PPS, and it weighs 513 g.
 The Amazon title does not print UGREEN’s model number. PCWorld links this same listing to the 145W bank with 140 W from one port, but some retailers list a different port split, so check the 145W label and the port markings when it arrives. It sells for about $80, so check the live price before you buy.
 Pack the INIU 65W for a travel router and phone
 A travel router does not need a 140 W bank. GL.iNet rates the Beryl AX at under 8 W and the Beryl 7 at under 12 W. The INIU’s 65 W port has room for the router, your phone and a 13-inch ultrabook, and at 324 g it weighs about half as much as the 140 W banks.
 INIU 20000mAh 65W (P62-E1): 65 W USB-C in a 324 g bank. Image: INIU. 
 Made for you if you carry a travel router, a phone and maybe a small laptop, and you want the lightest bank that still charges a laptop. Look elsewhere if your laptop shipped with a 100 W or 140 W charger. Under load it will charge slowly or not at all from a 65 W port.
 INIU’s page for the P62-E1 lists 65 W on the first USB-C port (20 V at 3.25 A), 36 W on the second and 18 W on USB-A, with 60 W total. Input is 45 W, PPS is among the protocols, and a 100 W cable and a three-year warranty come with it. Both USB-C ports together drop to 45 W and 20 W, which still leaves the router plenty.
 INIU does not publish the PPS voltage range or the Wh rating online, so read the Wh figure printed on the bank before you fly with it. The Amazon title also lacks the model number. The name, capacity and weight are what tie it to the P62-E1.
 INIU did recall a power bank in December 2025, but it was the BI-B41, not this model. It sells for about $42, so check the live price before you buy.
 Feed 12 V barrel-jack gear from the Talentcell
 Some gear never got a USB-C input. Cellular routers built for a van and 12 V network switches take a 5.5 mm barrel plug. The Talentcell feeds them 12 V directly instead of through an adapter cable.
 Talentcell PB030201-35: 76.65 Wh, 12 V DC out plus 45 W USB-C. Image: Talentcell. 
 Right for you if you run a 12 V device, such as the GL.iNet Spitz Plus that our travel router guide lists with a 9 to 36 V input. Look elsewhere if your mini PC uses a 19 V or 20 V barrel jack, which most do. This bank only outputs 12 V on its DC side.
 Talentcell’s page for the PB030201-35 lists 76.65 Wh, a 45 W USB-C PD port, an 18 W USB-A port and a DC5521 one-to-two splitter, and it links to this exact Amazon listing. It recharges from its own 12.6 V barrel charger rather than over USB-C.
 The page lists that charger at 1 A while the Amazon title says 2 A. Its technical details tab is an image with no text, so we could not confirm the maximum 12 V output current. Check your device’s input current against the label before you rely on it. It sells for about $50, so check the live price before you buy.
 Work out runtime for a router, Pi or mini PC
 You can estimate runtime from two numbers: what the bank delivers and what the device draws. Use about 75 Wh for the Anker 737 and about 80 Wh for the Anker Prime 26K, the low end of each measured range. For the device, the maker’s maximum rating gives you a worst case:
 Device Power input Draw used Anker 737 (75 Wh) Anker Prime 26K (80 Wh) 
 GL.iNet Brume 2 (GL-MT2500A) 5 V 2 A under 2.6 W (max) about 29 h about 31 h 
 GL.iNet Beryl AX (GL-MT3000) 5 V 3 A under 8 W (max) about 9 h about 10 h 
 GL.iNet Beryl 7 (GL-MT3600BE) 5 V 3 A, 9 V 3 A, 12 V 2.5 A under 12 W (max, no USB load) about 6 h about 6.5 h 
 GL.iNet Slate 7 (GL-BE3600) 5 V 3 A, 9 V 3 A, 12 V 2.5 A under 18 W (max, no USB load) about 4 h about 4.5 h 
 Raspberry Pi 5, idle 5 V 5 A recommended about 3 W about 25 h about 27 h 
 Intel N150 mini PC with USB-C power input, idle USB-C PD (most use a barrel jack) 7 to 11 W about 7 to 11 h about 7 to 11 h 
 Read the router hours as a floor, because GL.iNet’s figures are maximum draw and a router moving light traffic sits well below them. The two low-draw rows are the least certain: the 75 and 80 Wh figures were measured at 20 to 28 V, and some banks switch their output off when a 2 to 3 W load looks like nothing is plugged in.
 The Pi 5 and N150 idle figures come from our Raspberry Pi 5 vs N150 comparison , and they rise fast under load.
 Say you run a GL.iNet Tailscale setup on a Beryl 7 through a long travel day. INIU publishes no Wh figure, but 20,000 mAh at a typical 3.6 to 3.7 V cell voltage is about 72 to 74 Wh, and at 80 to 85 percent delivery that’s roughly five hours at full draw. Treat that as our estimate.
 Power a Raspberry Pi 5 or mini PC over USB-C
 A Raspberry Pi 5 boots from any power bank that gives 5 V at 3 A, but it won’t get its full USB power budget. The Raspberry Pi documentation recommends 5 V at 5 A (25 W). On a supply that can’t offer 5 A, the Pi limits its USB ports to 600 mA in total, against 1.6 A on a 5 A supply.
 Laptop power banks reach their higher watts by raising the voltage, not by offering 5 A at 5 V. None of the banks here lists the 5.1 V 5 A profile the Pi 5 needs for its full budget. The official 27 W Pi supply does it with a 5.1 V at 5 A profile.
 That 600 mA limit is fine for a headless Pi with an SD card. It bites when you hang a USB SSD off it. The docs describe usb_max_current_enable=1 in config.txt and the Pi 5 EEPROM setting PSU_MAX_CURRENT , which lift the limit. They are meant for supplies that can really deliver the current, so do not use them to push a 3 A bank past its rating. If your Pi needs USB storage on battery, power the drive separately. Our Raspberry Pi 5 kits guide covers the official supply.
 Mini PCs are harder, because most still use a barrel jack. ASUS lists a 19 V DC input on the NUC 15 Pro, for example. Minisforum’s UM790 Pro page lists a 19 V adapter and says its USB4 ports support PD power delivery. Before you buy a bank for a mini PC, check these:
 Your mini PC’s spec page says a USB-C port accepts power input, not only that it outputs power.
 The bank’s single-port rating is at least what the mini PC’s own adapter supplies, usually 65 W or more.
 You’ve read the barrel input voltage if you plan to use a USB-C trigger cable, because common PD steps are 5, 9, 12, 15 and 20 V with no 19 V step.
 You’ve confirmed with the maker that a 20 V feed is inside the input range of a 19 V box before you plug one in.
 The trigger cable route works on paper, but no maker we checked documents a 19 V mini PC on a 20 V feed. Treat it as your own risk. A USB-C powered mini PC on a 140 W bank is the cleaner setup, and our homelab mini PC guide covers the boxes worth running.
 Read PD wattage and PPS on the spec sheet
 USB Power Delivery tops out at 100 W (20 V at 5 A) in its standard range. PD 3.1 added 28 V for 140 W, 36 V for 180 W and 48 V for 240 W, according to the USB-IF charger page . Every 140 W port in this guide uses the 28 V step. It only works when the laptop asks for it and the cable can carry it. A spec sheet worth trusting answers these lines:
 You can find the single-port maximum, written as volts and amps (28 V 5 A), not only the total across ports.
 You can see what each port drops to when two devices share the bank.
 You know whether PPS is listed and over what voltage range, if your phone uses it.
 You know the recharge input wattage, which decides how fast the bank refills between flights.
 You can read a Wh rating, not only mAh.
 The cable is the part that trips people up. Anything over 3 A needs an e-marked 5 A cable, and 140 W needs one rated for the extended range, sold as 240 W. Plug a 60 W cable into a 140 W bank and your laptop quietly charges at 60 W.
 PPS, the programmable mode, lets a phone ask for voltage in small steps instead of fixed ones. Anker lists it as 3.3 to 21 V at 5 A on its Prime 27,650mAh 250W model. It matters for phones, not laptops, so do not pay extra for it unless your phone’s fast mode depends on it.
 Learn the 2026 airline rules for power banks
 Every regulator agrees on the basics. Power banks travel in the cabin, never in checked bags, and under 100 Wh needs no approval. The FAA PackSafe page still allows two spares of 101 to 160 Wh with airline approval, but IATA’s 2026 guidance puts power banks in their own class. Most of what changed since 2025 is about using the bank on board:
 Rule maker In force What it means for you 
 ICAO / IATA 27 March 2026 Two power banks per person, cabin only, no recharging them on board; using one to charge a device is discouraged. 100 to 160 Wh power banks lose the approval route in the IATA DGR from 1 January 2027. 
 FAA / TSA (US) Current Carry-on only, 100 Wh limit, two spares of 101 to 160 Wh with airline approval. 
 Southwest Airlines 20 April 2026 (visible-use rule since 2025) One power bank, 100 Wh max, not in the overhead bin, no recharging from seat power, visible while in use. 
 Emirates 1 October 2025 No use on board at all; one bank under 100 Wh; not in the overhead bin. 
 Qantas and Jetstar 15 December 2025 No use or charging, including from seat power; two banks of up to 160 Wh each. 
 Virgin Australia 1 December 2025 No use and no recharging from aircraft power; two banks. 
 Singapore Airlines and Scoot In force by October 2026 No use and no charging on board. 
 China CAAC (domestic flights) 28 June 2025 Banks without a valid 3C mark, with an unclear label, or under recall are refused at security. 
 For your buying decision, a 99 Wh bank is the biggest you should buy. The 100 to 160 Wh tier is shrinking, and Emirates already allows only one bank under 100 Wh. On many long-haul carriers you can no longer charge a laptop from a bank mid-flight, so seat power does that job and the bank covers the layover and the hotel.
 The IATA guidance PDF has the full table. Your airline’s own page wins over all of this.
 Check these before you board
 Most airport trouble with a power bank comes down to a label nobody can read or a rule you didn’t know your airline had. Run through this list the night before you fly:
 You can read the Wh rating printed on the bank itself, and it’s under 100 Wh.
 You’re carrying no more than two power banks, or one on Emirates and Southwest.
 Your bank is in your carry-on and your checked bag holds none.
 You’ve checked your airline’s page for an in-flight use ban and an overhead bin rule.
 Your bank shows a 3C mark if you’re flying within China.
 You’ve packed a 240 W rated USB-C cable if your laptop charges at 140 W.
 You’ve charged the bank at home, since recharging it on board isn’t allowed under the 2026 rules.
 If your model is not one of the six above, the same list still tells you whether it can fly. The Wh line matters most, because a bank with a worn or missing label can be refused even when it is well under the limit. Clear tape over the label keeps it readable after a year in a bag.  Eight USB-C power banks that can charge a laptop at 100 W or more, checked for October 2026, with capacity in mAh and Wh and the FAA and TSA carry-on rules explained.
 Andrei Budai 
 October 5, 2026
 The best power banks for laptops in 2026 put out 65 W or more over USB-C Power Delivery and hold close to the 100 Wh airline limit. For most people the Anker Laptop Power Bank (25K, 165W) is the one to buy. It charges a laptop at up to 100 W, has two built-in USB-C cables, and Anker markets it as flight-approved.
 This guide is for people who work away from an outlet: on flights, trains, job sites and long days on campus. A phone-size power bank will not do the job. Laptops need higher voltage and far more energy, so the short list below only includes models their makers rate for 100 W or more.
 Last checked October 2026: availability, specs and prices. 
 What to Look for in Power Banks for Laptops
 Single-port wattage, not the total. The big number on the box is usually the combined output of all ports. What matters for a laptop is what one USB-C port can deliver. Check the wattage printed on your laptop’s own charger and match it. A 100 W port covers most thin-and-light and mid-size laptops. Laptops that ship with 140 W chargers need a port rated at 140 W to charge at full speed.
 Capacity in watt-hours. Milliamp-hours (mAh) are a poor guide for laptops, because the figure depends on the voltage it is quoted at. Watt-hours (Wh) tell you the real energy. The FAA gives the formula: multiply the battery voltage by the amp-hours. Expect less at the laptop than the label says. Anker’s own product pages put conversion losses at roughly 30% to 45%.
 The airline carry-on limit. The TSA says power banks must be packed in carry-on bags and are prohibited in checked luggage. The FAA limits lithium-ion batteries to 100 Wh each. With airline approval, a passenger may carry up to two larger spares of 101 to 160 Wh. The FAA also notes that airlines may set stricter limits, so check with yours. Every pick below is sold as being under the 100 Wh line.
 Recharge speed. A big battery is slow to refill through a weak input. Look for 65 W input or better. The fastest models here take 100 W or more.
 Weight and shape. Laptop-class power banks weigh from about 390 g to 630 g. Most are brick-shaped. One pick is flat, which matters if it rides in a laptop sleeve.
 Cables and display. Built-in cables mean one less thing to forget. A display that shows watts in and out helps you confirm the laptop is really charging at the speed you paid for.
 Best Power Banks for Laptops: Our Picks
 All eight were in stock on their makers’ own stores when checked. Capacity is given in mAh and, where the maker publishes it, in Wh.
 1. Anker Laptop Power Bank (25K, 165W)
 The Anker Laptop Power Bank (25K, 165W) has a 25,000 mAh battery and three USB-C outputs: one port and two attached cables, which Anker describes as built-in and retractable. Each can deliver up to 100 W, and any two together share 165 W. There is also a 33 W USB-A port, so four devices can charge at once.
 Anker lists a 100 W input and says a full recharge takes about two hours with a 100 W charger. It weighs 595 g and has a screen that shows battery percentage and port status. Anker’s page gives the capacity in mAh only and labels the pack flight-approved, so check the Wh figure printed on the unit before you fly. It costs about $120 (October 2026).
 Pros of the Anker 25K 165W
 Up to 100 W from each USB-C output
 Two attached USB-C cables, so there is nothing extra to pack
 100 W input for a recharge in about two hours
 Cons of the Anker 25K 165W
 Tops out at 100 W per port, short of 140 W laptops
 Wh rating is not shown on the product page
 2. UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 25000mAh 200W
 The UGREEN Nexode 25000mAh 200W is the pick for laptops with 140 W chargers. UGREEN lists the capacity as 25,000 mAh (90 Wh). The first USB-C port delivers up to 140 W over PD 3.1 and the second up to 100 W, so it can run two laptops at once. A USB-A port handles a phone.
 The TFT display shows remaining battery, voltage, current, input and output in real time. The pack weighs 609 g. Its weak point is the 65 W input, which is modest for a battery this size. The list price is about $130 (October 2026).
 Pros of the UGREEN 200W
 140 W from one USB-C port, 100 W from the other
 90 Wh capacity stated by the maker
 Detailed real-time display
 Cons of the UGREEN 200W
 65 W maximum input
 At 609 g, one of the heavier packs here
 3. Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W)
 The Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) is the high-end choice. Anker states 26,250 mAh (99.75 Wh), which sits just under the FAA’s 100 Wh line. Each of its two USB-C ports delivers up to 140 W, a USB-A port adds 22.5 W, and total output reaches 300 W.
 Recharging is the standout. Anker says the pack accepts up to 250 W through both USB-C ports together and reaches 50% in 13 minutes, a figure from its own lab tests that requires two 140 W chargers and 5 A cables. It weighs 600 g, has a smart display and can be controlled from an app. The price is about $230 (October 2026).
 Pros of the Anker Prime 26K
 Two 140 W USB-C ports
 99.75 Wh, close to the most you can fly with unapproved
 Very fast dual-port recharging, per Anker
 Cons of the Anker Prime 26K
 Costs about twice as much as the other picks
 Top recharge speed needs two 140 W chargers
 4. UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 25000mAh 165W
 The UGREEN Nexode 25000mAh 165W is UGREEN’s answer to the Anker at the top of this list. It has two built-in braided USB-C cables and can charge up to four devices at once from a 25,000 mAh pack that UGREEN rates at 90 Wh.
 UGREEN lists 90 W fast recharging and says a full refill takes about two hours. An LED display shows the remaining battery. The list price is about $110 (October 2026), and UGREEN’s store showed a coupon code below that when checked.
 Pros of the UGREEN 165W
 Two built-in braided USB-C cables
 90 Wh stated capacity
 Recharges in about two hours, per UGREEN
 Cons of the UGREEN 165W
 Simpler display than the 200 W model
 Built-in cables cannot be swapped if they wear out
 5. INIU Cougar P63 (25,000 mAh, 100W)
 The INIU Cougar P63 is the light one. INIU lists it at 392 g and 11 x 7 x 3.6 cm, and claims it is 30% smaller than other 25,000 mAh, 100 W packs. For a bag you carry all day, that difference is easy to feel.
 The main USB-C port delivers up to 100 W and takes up to 65 W in. A second USB-C port is rated at 45 W and the USB-A port at 18 W. INIU does not print a Wh figure for this model on its page. It says its power banks range from 37 Wh to 99.9 Wh, all under 100 Wh. The price was about $67 (October 2026).
 Pros of the INIU P63
 392 g, far lighter than the other 25,000 mAh picks
 100 W from the main USB-C port
 Lowest price among the 25,000 mAh models
 Cons of the INIU P63
 Output drops when several ports are in use
 No model-specific Wh figure on the product page
 6. UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 20000mAh 130W
 The UGREEN Nexode 20000mAh 130W trades some capacity for size. UGREEN lists 20,000 mAh (72 Wh) and a weight of 476 g. The first USB-C port delivers up to 100 W, the second 30 W, and the USB-A port 22.5 W.
 Input is 65 W and the display is the same TFT type as the 200 W model. With 72 Wh on board it will not fully refill a large laptop, but it is a sensible size for a 13-inch or 14-inch machine. The list price is about $90 (October 2026).
 Pros of the UGREEN 130W
 100 W USB-C port in a 476 g pack
 72 Wh, well under the airline limit
 TFT display
 Cons of the UGREEN 130W
 Second USB-C port is only 30 W
 Less energy than the 25,000 mAh picks
 7. Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K)
 The Anker 737 Power Bank is an older design that Anker still sells, and it remains a straightforward way to get 140 W. It has a 24,000 mAh battery, two USB-C ports and one USB-A port, with 140 W maximum output and 140 W two-way charging through USB-C.
 It weighs 630 g and has a smart digital display. Anker’s page lists the capacity in mAh only. It costs about $110 (October 2026).
 Pros of the Anker 737
 140 W USB-C output and input
 Long-running model with hundreds of owner reviews on Anker’s store
 Cons of the Anker 737
 Heaviest pick at 630 g
 No built-in cables
 Wh rating is not shown on the product page
 8. Baseus Blade H1 (20,000 mAh, 100W)
 The Baseus Blade H1 is the flat one. Baseus lists it at 1.8 cm thick and about 451 g, a shape that slides into a laptop sleeve where a brick will not.
 It has a 20,000 mAh battery, four ports, 100 W maximum output, a digital display and pass-through charging. Baseus lists a 60 W input and a charge time of 1.5 hours. The page does not give a Wh figure. It was priced at about $90 (October 2026).
 Pros of the Baseus Blade H1
 Thin, flat body that packs next to a laptop
 100 W output and four ports
 Cons of the Baseus Blade H1
 Larger footprint than a brick-style pack
 No Wh figure on the product page
 Laptop Power Bank Questions
 Can I take a laptop power bank on a plane?
 Yes, in your carry-on only. The TSA prohibits power banks in checked bags. The FAA limit is 100 Wh per battery without approval, and up to two spares of 101 to 160 Wh with airline approval. If a carry-on is gate-checked, the FAA says power banks must be removed and kept with you in the cabin.
 How many watts does my laptop need?
 Read the output printed on the charger that came with it. A power bank with a lower rating will often still charge the laptop, just more slowly, and may not keep up under heavy load.
 How many times will a 25,000 mAh power bank charge a laptop?
 Usually about once. A 25,000 mAh pack holds around 90 Wh, and some of that is lost in conversion. Anker says its 99.75 Wh Prime model charges a MacBook Pro (M4) up to 0.8 times.
 Do I need a special cable?
 For 100 W and above, yes. Use a USB-C cable rated for 5 A, or 240 W for a 140 W port. An ordinary phone cable will limit the charging speed.

 Conclusion
 Buy the Anker Laptop Power Bank (25K, 165W) if your laptop charges at 100 W or less: the built-in cables and fast recharge make it the easiest to live with. If your laptop came with a 140 W charger, choose the UGREEN Nexode 200W , or the Anker Prime 26K if you also want the fastest recharge and the most capacity you can fly with.
 Travelers who count grams should look at the INIU Cougar P63 , and the Baseus Blade H1 suits anyone who wants a flat pack in a laptop sleeve. For a smaller laptop, the 72 Wh UGREEN Nexode 130W is enough.

 Buy the wrong power bank for your laptop and it won't actually charge it. It'll just slow the drain while you work.
 That's the trap: a bank's mAh number tells you nothing about whether it can keep up with your laptop's power draw.
 What actually matters is watts in versus watts out.
 After testing across MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, and Windows ultrabooks, the Anker 737 Power Bank came out as the best overall pick for laptop charging. It's the only mainstream bank that hits the full 140W a 16-inch MacBook Pro needs, with a live display that shows exactly what's being delivered.
 Critical Wattage Thresholds
 Your laptop's charging wattage determines which power bank class you need:
 MacBook Air M2 (70W max) : any 65W+ power bank charges it, though 65W will be slightly slower than a wall adapter. A 100W bank charges it at maximum rated speed.
 MacBook Pro 14-inch (96W max) : a 65W power bank slows (but does not stop) discharge under heavy load. A 100W bank charges it near maximum speed.
 MacBook Pro 16-inch (140W max) : a 100W power bank charges it slowly while in light use; under heavy load the laptop still discharges. Only 140W+ banks (Anker 737) charge it at full speed.
 Windows gaming laptops (100-230W max) : most gaming laptops cannot be fully charged from USB-PD power banks while gaming. Power banks extend usage time but do not replace the brick adapter for gaming.
 What "Pass-Through" Means
 Pass-through charging means the power bank can charge itself from the wall while simultaneously outputting power to connected devices. This is useful for situations where you have one outlet and multiple devices.
 Not all pass-through implementations are equal: some reduce output wattage significantly while charging the bank (charging at 100W out + 65W in might drop output to 45W). Check reviews for real-world pass-through watt measurements.
 The Anker 737 supports pass-through effectively — confirmed through our watt-meter measurements.
 The Airline Restriction Reality
 The relevant number for airline carry-on compliance is Wh, not mAh. The 100Wh limit is approximately 27,000mAh at the standard 3.7V cell voltage.
 All three recommended banks (Anker 737: 88.8Wh, Baseus Blade: 74Wh, INIU BI-B70: 74Wh) fit under the 100Wh carry-on limit. They can be brought on any commercial flight without special approval.
 If you find a 30,000mAh or 40,000mAh power bank: calculate the Wh before buying. These typically exceed 100Wh and require airline-specific approval or may not be permitted.
 Self-Recharge Time for Travel Use
 On a one-day business trip, you may need to recharge the power bank itself:
 Anker 737 (65W input): approximately 2.5 hours to full
 Baseus Blade (45W input): approximately 3.5-4 hours to full
 INIU BI-B70 (45W input): approximately 4-5 hours to full
 For multi-day trips: any of these self-recharge overnight in a hotel room. For single-day turnarounds: the Anker 737's 65W input is the most practical.

 The best laptop power banks for 2026
 These portable laptop chargers will keep your computer alive when you're far from an outlet.
 By   Amy Skorheim 
 Updated: Jan. 12, 2026 5:01 am EST

 Laptop power banks come in handy if you often travel or work away from your desk. These larger batteries have enough capacity to refill your computer to around 75 percent, giving you many more productive hours. Of course, they can also charge smaller devices like your phone, camera or tablet a few times over. Nearly all portable laptop chargers fall below the 100-watt-hour mark so you can bring them in your carry-on when you fly. Additional features, like built-in cables and digital displays make these battery banks easier to use, too. We tested over a dozen options and put our thoughts below, so you can find the best laptop power bank for your next trip away from an outlet.

 Best laptop power overall
 Anker Laptop Power Bank 25K 
 Capacity : 25,000mAh, 90 Wh | Ports : Two built-in USB-C in/out cables, one USB-A port, one USB-C port | Cable : USB-C to USB-C | Number of charges iPhone 15 : 4 – 5 | Charge time iPhone : 5 to 100% in 1h 54m | Number of charges Galaxy S23 Ultra : 3.75 – 4 | Charge time S23 Ultra : 52m | Number of charges iPad Air : 1.75 – 2 | Charge time iPad : 5 to 100% in 1h 58m | Number of charges MacBook Pro : 0.68 | Charge time MacBook Pro : 53 m
 My favorite new feature for power banks is the built-in cable. This Anker laptop power bank sports two: one attached to the side of the battery that doubles as a carrying strap and another retractable cord that extends up to two feet. Both are USB-C and can accommodate in/out charges so you can use them to refill a device or reup the battery itself.
 The brick has a display to tell you the amount of charge remaining, as well as the output wattage that's funneling towards your devices from each port. When refilling the battery, you can see an estimate of how long it will be until the unit is full. Calculating and displaying info like that takes up a bit of power but, in my testing, the battery output the same or a higher amount of charge compared with other 25,000 mAh packs.
 The 25,000 mAh capacity isn't as high as other TSA-compatible power banks, but sacrificing those few extra percentage points for this bank's speed, convenience and great price is definitely worth it.

 Best laptop power bank for travel
 Lion Energy Eclipse Mag 
 174 149 
 Capacity : 27,000 mAh, 99.9 Wh | Ports : One USB-C in/out, two USB-A out and three wireless pads | Cable included : USB-C to USB-C and wall adapter | Charge time iPhone 15 : 5 to 100% in 2h 56m (wireless) 5 – 100% 2h 22m (wired) | Remaining charge after iPhone : ~ 81% | Charge time Galaxy S23 Ultra : 5 to 100% in 1h 20m | Remaining charge after S23 Ultra : ~ 77% | Charge time iPad Air : 5 to 100% in 1h 55m | Remaining charge after iPad : ~ 64% | Charge time MacBook Pro : 10% to 89% in 1h 18m
 Traveling is one of the top reasons people need to use a portable laptop charger — planes, trains, buses and airports aren't exactly the easiest places to find a power source. Lion Energy's Eclipse Mag battery pack has a big 27,000 capacity, which is enough to power a laptop through a couple days of use. I also like how its three wireless charging pads cut down on cable chaos, letting you charge a Qi-enabled phone, earbuds case and Apple Watch at the same time.
 You certainly could charge all three of those accessories and a laptop at one time, but as with all batteries, that increased drain will quickly empty it and your charge times will slow down quite a bit. From what I've seen, the unit works best as an as-needed power supply when you're out and about, then, after a recharge, it can moonlight as a three-in-one wireless charger in your hotel room. You can even rely on the pass-through charging capabilities to power up the battery while using the wireless pads, making it a sort of travel-ready multi-device charger .
 At two pounds, no one would call this light, but the angled corners and narrow design make it feel more compact than other big batteries. There's no display to tell you how much charge is left, just four lighted pips at one edge, but I found them to provide a fairly accurate estimate. One thing to note is that the wireless watch pad only works with Apple Watches. Since Pixel watches don't support wireless charging and Samsung only recommends its own chargers for Galaxy Watches, that's not surprising. 
 The only other drawback is the single USB-C port. The three wireless pads and the two USB-A ports will likely be enough for a days' work, but one more type-C port would be ideal. Compared to other 27,000 maAh battery packs, the $174 price tag on the Eclipse Mag is a decent deal — and it even comes with a five-year warranty.

 Wireless charging is convenient for travel
 Compact design for such a large battery
 Delivers a fast, 79 percent charge to a large laptop

 Anker's latest Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) is particularly high-end. It delivers up to 300 watts of power (combined), has an optional drop-and-go charging base and Bluetooth connectivity lets you monitor its functions through an app. That last bit is honestly more of a fun novelty than actually practical, but the battery itself is plenty useful.
 The three ports can be used all at once, with the two USB-C ports delivering up to 140 watts each. That's not a scenario that's likely to happen often, as most devices charge far below that level. My MacBook Pro recharged at around 90 watts for most of my test. But, if you happen to have two high-powered laptops it's possible you might take advantage of all that power.
 It was able to deliver more power to my MacBook Pro than any other battery I've tested. My laptop went from 10 to 75 percent in about 45 minutes, which is the fastest time I've tracked. As for smaller devices, it charged an iPhone from nearly dead to over 60 percent in about a half hour.
 Anker made the battery a little wider and flatter than the last round of Prime devices, and it's a bit more compact than most 27,000mAh batteries out there. The onboard display not only tells you how much charge is left in the battery, it also has a temperature gauge — a wise thing to keep an eye on when it comes to lithium ion batteries.
 The display also shows a cute little animation when you plonk the battery on the base. Of course, the charging base isn't necessary, but it does make recharging the battery super convenient — plus it has extra ports to act as a mini charging station. Since the base itself costs $110, you're looking at more than $300 for the whole set, but if speed is what you want for your laptop's recharge, it's the way to go.

 I hadn't even heard of Baseus before I started testing products for these guides. But after reading the many positive reviews, I gave a few of the brand's offerings a try and have been repeatedly impressed by their value-to-performance ratio. The Baseus Blade is a compact and flat battery that weighs just over a pound. The shape is more tablet-like than the standard block of most power banks, which makes it easier to slide into a backpack or messenger bag alongside a laptop — it's also the lightest of the banks I tried in this capacity category. 
 The display underestimates the amount of charge left, which is always better than the alternative. When the Blade was down to just one percent, it gave my laptop a few more percentage points before giving up the ghost. It has two USB-C and two USB-A ports along with little feet at the bottom that keep from moving around as you plug charging cables into it. The speeds were admirable, clocking in just a few minutes longer than batteries with larger capacities.
 That's the main trade off here: At 20,000 mAh, it's not going to deliver the same amount of charge as a bigger bank. It boosted my 16-inch MacBook Pro from 10 percent to 62 percent, which is about 20 percentage points lower than the bigger batteries could do. But for $100, it's still a speedy portable charger with a convenient shape and a good number of ports.

 Best laptop power bank for the outdoors
 Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC 
 Capacity : 25,600 mAh, 95Wh | Ports : One USB-C in/out, one USB-C out, one USB-C in, two USB-A, one AC port, one solar input and one wireless pad | Cable : USB-C to USB-C | Charge time iPhone 15 : 0 to 100% in 1h 49m | Remaining charge after iPhone : 83% | Charge time Galaxy S23 Ultra : 5 to 100% in 1h 3m | Remaining charge after S23 Ultra : 77% | Charge time iPad Air : 4 to 100% in 2h 11m | Remaining charge after iPad : 62% | Charge time MacBook Pro : 6% to 72% in 1h 21m
 Let's get the bad news out of the way first: Goal Zero's Sherpa 100AC costs $250. That makes it the most expensive power bank I've tested so far. But it's a high-quality unit that gives you what you pay for. There's a wireless charging pad up top, three USB-C ports (though one is input only), plus a couple of USB-A ports, an AC port and an 8mm port that can pair up with a Goal Zero solar panel or 12V adapter cable to recharge from your car. There's even an internal fan to keep everything cool as it deals with all the output and a status display you can turn on or off.
 Goal Zero is probably best known for its outdoor-focused power products — power stations for camping, portable solar panels and camping lights, to name a few. The Sherpa has the same rugged/industrial aluminum unibody design, which would make it an ideal productivity companion for field work. I could see this coming in handy for outdoor photo shoots, job-site projects or just snagging some nature-side office hours.
 The ability to recharge from a car's 12V port or even from solar panels is another nice-to-have, but of course, you'll need extra equipment. In the case of the car charger, that's another $40, but the solar panels will add another $250 to your mobile set up. If you find yourself working out in the field relatively often you might appreciate the flexibility.

 UGreen

 UGreen Power Bank 25,000mAh 145W 
 UGreen's 25,000mAh power bank is a compact, low-frills bank that delivers a speedy charge to smartphones — my tester iPhone 15 in particular. I clocked a refill from four percent to full in about an hour and a half. That's among the faster speeds from any power bank I've tested and is thanks to its 145W max output. It performed on par with other bricks when it came to refilling a Galaxy Ultra, iPad Air and MacBook Pro.
 A small digital display indicates the amount of charge left and it tested accurately. There are just three ports — two USB-C and one Type-A — but that's more than enough to handle a laptop and a smartphone at the same time, if you must. But I've found portable chargers work best when handling just one device at a time. Adding an extra device seems to drain it quicker than charging one then another.
 Upon its debut, the UGreen Power Bank 25,000mAh went for $120 so the value wasn't quite there. But now it's been reduced to an MSRP of $100 and is regularly on UGreen's site and Amazon for around $75. I've noticed some in-stock issues, but if you can find it, snap it up. It's a high-performing, low-frills battery with a surprising amount of oomph for its compact size.
 See at Amazon 
 What to look for in a laptop power bank
 Flying with a laptop power bank 
 Most portable batteries top out at around 27,000mAh so you can fly with them. The TSA currently limits the capacity carry-on batteries to 100Wh, which works out to around 27,500mAh for 3.6 volt lithium-ion batteries. Note that you're not allowed to pack any batteries in your checked luggage, regardless of capacity. The TSA rules are intended to limit fire danger — and some airlines are implementing further restrictions due to recent on-board incidents.
 In March 2025, a Hong Kong flight was grounded after a battery pack caught fire in an overhead bin. A similar situation happened that same year in July on a domestic Delta flight, and again in August on a transatlantic KLM flight . As a result, some airlines, including Emirates , Southwest and others have announced further restrictions on flying with battery packs.
 Rules include limiting the number of allowed portable chargers and requiring flyers to keep power banks in clear view when using them to recharge a device. If the battery pack isn't actively in use, however, most rules allow them to stay in your carry-on bag in the overhead bin. Before flying, it's wise to check your airline's policies.
 Capacity 
 If you just need to keep a smartphone from dying before you can make it home, just about any of the best power banks will do . But if you need to revive multiple devices or the substantial battery of a laptop, you'll want something with a high milliamp-hour​​ (mAh) capacity. A power bank capable of delivering enough power to a laptop will have a capacity between 20,000 and 27,000 mAh.
 If you want something even bigger than a laptop power bank, and don't need to fly with it, you'll likely want to look into portable power stations. These can be the size of a car battery or larger and can potentially fuel an entire weekend away.
 Another thing to keep in mind is that the capacity listed in a power bank's specs is not what will be delivered to your devices. As I mentioned, the capacity of these banks is around 25,000mAh. Even the huge battery on a 16-inch MacBook Pro or a Dell XPS 16 has a mAh rating of around 5,000 – 6,000mAh, so you might think you'd get five full charges but in reality, you only get about a single 70-percent charge. The voltage is different (typically 3.7V for the power bank and 11.4V for a laptop) which makes the watt-hours, or the amount of energy each battery can hold, different (working out to 92Wh for the battery and 72Wh for the built-in laptop batteries). On top of that, in order to feed a charge from a power bank to a laptop, a voltage conversion takes place and that dissipates a decent amount of energy.
 Without turning this into a physics lesson, this all means that a power bank with a 25,000mAh (or 92Wh) capacity will typically fill a 5,000mAh (or 72Wh) laptop battery to about 75 percent. In my tests, I averaged about a 60-percent efficiency rate between a power bank's listed capacity and the actual charge delivered.
 Ports 
 Every large power bank I've tested has at least three USB ports, with a mix of USB-C and USB-A, which should cover nearly any portable device you need to recharge — earbuds, phones, tablets, laptops, you name it. In addition to the different plug formats, some ports supply power at different wattages. For example, one built-in USB-C port might be rated for 60 watts, while the one next to it is rated for 100 watts. So if you've got a device that's capable of 70W fast charging, such as the new MacBook Air, you'd want to opt for the 100W port to get the best charging speeds possible. 
 Note that devices with a smaller wattage draw won't be negatively affected by connecting to ports with high ratings. For example, a Galaxy S24 Ultra, capable of 45W super fast charging, is perfectly compatible with the 100W port. A device will only draw what it can take, regardless of what a port can supply. Just remember that the port, device and charging cable need to be at or above the desired wattage rating to achieve maximum charging rates.
 Some of these larger batteries also have AC ports. It might seem like a natural fit to plug in your laptop's power adapter for a recharge. But really, the AC port should only be for devices that can't use USB — such as a lamp or a printer. Plugging a power adapter into the AC port only wastes energy through conversion. First, the battery converts its DC power to supply the port with AC power, then the power adapter converts that AC power back to DC so your laptop can take it in. And as you'll remember from physics class, each time energy is converted, some is lost to heat and other dissipations. Better to cut out the middleman and just send that DC power straight from the battery to the device.
 Also, you can use more than one port at a time with these devices; just remember that the speed of whatever you're charging will likely go down, and of course, the battery is going to drain proportionally to what you're refilling.
 Wireless charging 
 Since I first started testing portable power banks a few years ago, wireless charging capabilities have noticeably improved. The first few I tried were painfully slow and not worth recommending. Now the wireless pads built into power banks are impressively fast — particularly, in my experience, when charging Samsung Galaxy phones (though the lack of a stabilizing magnetic connection like Apple's MagSafe means they only work when rested flat on a pad). Most wireless charging connections can be used while other ports are also being employed, making them convenient for some mobile battlestation setups.
 Of course, wireless charging is always less efficient than wired, and recharging from an external battery is less efficient in general. If you want to waste as little energy as possible, you're better off sticking to wired connections.
 Design 
 All power banks are designed to be portable, but there's a big difference between a pocket-friendly 5,000mAh battery and one of these laptop-compatible bruisers. Most of the latter weigh between a pound and a half to two pounds, which is a considerable addition to a backpack. Many of the options listed here have a display to tell you how much charge remains in the battery, which is helpful when you're trying to judiciously meet out charges to your devices. If a bank has a wireless connection, the pad is usually on the flat top and any available AC connection is usually at one end. Both may require you to engage those charging methods. Don't be like me and grumble loudly that you got a bum unit without pressing (and sometimes double pressing) all the buttons first.
 How we test portable laptop chargers
 For the past three years, I've been testing and using dozens of portable batteries for our other battery guide . Some of those batteries include the higher-capacity power banks you see here. I also got a hold of a few extra banks just for this guide to make sure we covered what's available. I went for brands I'm already familiar with, as well as battery packs from well-received manufacturers I hadn't tried before (like UGREEN and Lion Energy). I only considered banks with at least a 20,000mAh capacity and mostly stuck with those that rated 25,000mAh and higher.
 Here's everything we tested:
 Zendure Supertank Pro 
 Mophie Powerstation Pro XL 
 Mophie Powerstation Pro AC 
 Lion Energy Eclipse Mag 
 Lion Energy Trek 
 Baseus Blade Laptop 
 Anker Prime 27,650mAh 
 Goal Zero Sherpa 100 AC 
 Anker Retractable Cable Laptop Bank 
 HyperJuice 245W 
 Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) 
 UGreen Power Bank 25,000mAh 145W  
 I tested each power bank with an Apple phone (iPhone 15 or 16), an Android phone (Galaxy S23 Ultra), a tablet (M1 iPad Air) and a laptop (16-inch MacBook Pro with the M1 Pro chip). Even though these banks can charge multiple devices at once, I refilled one at a time, to make side-by-side comparisons more straightforward. I drained the batteries of the phones and tablets to between zero and five percent and then didn't use any device as it refilled.
 For the MacBook, I let it run down to 10 percent before plugging in the power bank. That's when most laptops give display a "connect to power" warning, as draining any battery to empty will compromise the battery life. I then used it as one might in a mobile office, with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse, while connected to Wi-Fi and a VPN.
 For each test, I noted how long a completely charged battery took to get a device back to full and how much of the battery's capacity was used up in one charge. I also noted things like portability, apparent durability, helpful features and overall design.
 For reference, here are the battery capacities of the devices I used:
 iPhone 15: 3,349mAh
 Galaxy S23 Ultra: 4,855mAh
 iPad Air (5th gen): 7,729mAh
 16-inch M1 Pro MacBook Pro: 27,027mAh
 Other laptop power banks we tested
 HyperJuice 245W 
 Hyper's HyperJuice 245W brick looks great and has a hefty 27,000mAh capacity. The four USB-C ports can combine to output 245W of power and it got my MacBook Pro from nearly dead to 75 percent before depleting itself. When testing it with a Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra, the handset got back up to a full charge in just over an hour. The screen tells you what each port is doing as well as displaying the amount of charge remaining in the pack itself.
 But the lack of port variety makes it feel less versatile than other picks on this list — the price is higher than our other options, too.
 Laptop power bank FAQs
 How do laptop power banks differ from phone power banks? 
 The main difference is size. Phone power banks tend to have a capacity ranging from 5,000mAh to 20,000mAh and laptop powerbanks are typically rated between 20,000mAh and 27,000mAh. There's no official definition, however. Laptop batteries are simply larger and need a bigger supply of power to give them a meaningful charge.
 How do you fast charge a power bank? 
 You can charge a power bank exactly as fast as the power bank's internal mechanisms will allow. Most batteries are limited in how quickly they can accept and deliver a charge to avoid dangerously overheating. But to make sure you're charging a bank as quickly as possible, make sure the wall adapter and the USB-C cable you are using have a high wattage rating — using a 5W power brick and a 10W cable will take a lot longer to refill your bank than a 65W wall charger and a 100W cord.
 What size power bank do I need for a laptop? 
 Look for a power bank with a rating of at least 20,000mAh. Slightly smaller batteries may work, but they won't deliver a significant charge laptops.
 How many mAh to charge a laptop? 
 A milliamp hour (mAh) is how much a battery can hold, and most portable batteries list their capacity using mAh. If you get a battery rated at 20,000mAh or above, it should be able to charge your laptop.
 Using mAh to discuss laptop batteries can be confusing. Due to differing voltages, you can't directly compare the mAh ratings of a power bank battery to a laptop battery. Using watt-hours is a better gauge, as that calculation takes voltage into account.

 A phone power bank will not charge a laptop. The ones built for phones top out around 20 watts, and the moment you plug one into a USB-C laptop port the machine either refuses outright or charges at a trickle it will hold for a few minutes before going backwards. The best power banks for laptops are a different category of product, and the gap between a 20W pack and a 140W pack is not a price tier, it is the difference between an ornament and a working charger.
 Three numbers decide whether a pack works for your machine: output wattage (how hard it can push), capacity in watt-hours (how long it can keep pushing), and the USB-C Power Delivery profile it negotiates. Get those three right and almost anything with a USB-C port will charge. Get them wrong and you get the single most common complaint in buyer forums: a full pack that empties without ever completing a charge.
 Our answer up front: the Anker 737 Power Bank (140W, 24,000mAh) is the best power bank for laptops overall in 2026. It carries the highest review volume of any pack we looked at, its 140W USB-C output is enough to fast-charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the smart display on the front tells you exactly what the pack is doing instead of leaving you guessing.  How Many Watts Do I Need to Charge a Laptop?
 Match the pack’s single-port output to the charger your laptop shipped with. A Chromebook needs about 30W, a thin ultrabook 45W to 65W, a mainstream USB-C work laptop 100W, a 16-inch MacBook Pro or a gaming laptop 140W under Power Delivery 3.1, and a workstation-class machine 200W or more. Anything below your laptop’s rated adapter wattage will still charge it, but slowly, and often only while the machine is idle.
 The mistake buyers make is buying on capacity. A 25,000mAh pack with 65W output is a large battery that will feed a thin laptop at a third of its intended speed, and it will drain long before the laptop is full. Wattage is the first filter, capacity is the second.

 How Big a Power Bank Do You Need?
 Work in watt-hours, not milliamp-hours. A lithium cell sits at roughly 3.7V nominal, so a 25,000mAh pack holds about 92.5Wh of energy, and a 20,000mAh pack holds about 74Wh. The mAh figure is marketing; the Wh figure is the one the regulator and your laptop care about.
 For air travel, the FAA and most international regulators cap spare lithium batteries at 100Wh in carry-on baggage. That works out to roughly 27,000mAh at 3.7V, which is why nearly every pack in this roundup lands in the 20,000mAh to 27,650mAh band. Anything from 101Wh to 160Wh needs airline approval in advance, and anything above 160Wh is prohibited.
 Expect to receive less than the rated number. Conversion loss in the USB-C output stage means a 25,000mAh pack typically delivers somewhere in the region of 16,000mAh to a device, and the figure drops further if you use a long or thin cable.
 What Is USB-C Power Delivery and Does Every USB-C Cable Work?
 USB-C is only a connector shape. Power Delivery is the negotiation protocol that lets a laptop and a charger agree on a voltage and current profile, and a plain USB-C port or cable with no PD support cannot fast-charge anything. PD 2.0 tops out at 100W; PD 3.1 extends to 140W and 240W, which is why 140W laptop packs are a PD 3.1 feature.
 Every 100W or 140W pack here needs an e-marked 5A cable to actually deliver its headline number. A standard 3A cable will charge your laptop, just far more slowly, and several reviews in this roundup describe exactly that failure: a pack that seemed dead until a certified cable went in.
 PPS, or Programmable Power Supply, is a finer-grained version of PD that lets the charger adjust voltage in small steps, mostly benefiting phones and some laptops. Pass-through charging is the other term worth knowing: it lets the pack stay plugged in and power your laptop directly, acting roughly like a mini UPS, which is useful on a desk but means the pack never charges while it is doing it.
 Laptops You Cannot Power-Bank
 Some laptops simply cannot be charged from a power bank, and buying the wrong pack wastes money. Any machine that charges over a round barrel jack with a proprietary pin count is out, unless the manufacturer ships a USB-C adapter for it, and most gaming laptops with 180W or 230W bricks fall into that group.
 Even with USB-C, there is a ceiling. If your laptop’s adapter is 200W and the pack outputs 100W, the laptop will charge, but it will draw more power than the pack can replace while the machine is under load. Under sustained gaming or rendering it can hold charge and still lose ground, which is the behaviour owners describe as a full pack that empties without completing a charge.
 Two other causes produce the same symptom. Charging two devices at once splits the total output, so your laptop can drop from 100W to a fraction of that while the phone takes the rest. And a thin or non-e-marked cable adds voltage drop, so the pack is delivering full power and the laptop is receiving less.
 Our rule: match or exceed your adapter’s wattage, keep the pack on the laptop’s port alone when speed matters, and use a certified 5A cable above 100W.
