 Yes, with one hard limit: 100Wh maximum, in carry-on baggage only. Every pack in this roundup is rated under that ceiling, from the 20,000mAh AsperX at about 74Wh to the Anker Prime at 99.54Wh, so all ten fly without special permission.
 Never put a lithium power bank in a checked bag, regardless of size. Spare lithium batteries are not permitted in checked baggage because of the fire risk in a hold, and the rule applies to loose batteries and to power banks with built-in cells alike.
 For packs between 101Wh and 160Wh, airlines can approve them but the approval has to be obtained before you fly and the battery has to stay in the cabin. The protection circuit, terminals and casing condition all matter to the gate agent, and a damaged or swollen pack will be refused.
 Carry-on dimension limits apply too, so measure your bag first. The packs here run roughly 4.3 by 2.7 inches up to 6.6 by 3.2 inches, all of which fit a standard personal-item allowance on most carriers.
 Buying Guide: What to Check Before You Buy a Laptop Power Bank
 Per-port output versus total output
 The single most misunderstood number on the box is total output. A pack advertised at 145W might deliver 140W on one port and only 30W when a second device is plugged in, because the ceiling is shared. Read the port breakdown, not the headline figure, and if you will charge a laptop and a phone together, look for a pack that names separate per-port ratings.
 The UGREEN 200W model is the clearest example: 140W on USB-C1 and 100W on USB-C2 with a 200W combined ceiling. That layout charges a big laptop and a phone at full speed at the same time.
 Input wattage and recharge time
 Output is what you use during the day; input is what you deal with every night. A 25,000mAh pack refilling at 65W takes about two hours, while the same capacity at 140W input is done well under an hour. Several reviews here complain specifically about slow input, and it is the most fixable problem, since buying a higher-wattage wall charger often costs less than replacing the pack.
 Check that the pack accepts the charger you already own before buying a new one. Most list a 65W minimum for two-way fast charging.
 Real capacity versus rated capacity
 Rated capacity is measured at the cell and delivered capacity is what reaches your laptop after the DC-to-DC conversion stage and cable losses. Budget for roughly 65 to 75 percent of the rating in normal use. If a seller quotes a charge count for a named laptop, that figure already includes the losses and is the more honest number to plan around.
 Cable rating, more than anything else
 Above 100W, an e-marked 5A cable is not optional. Several owners in this roundup went from 6-7W to full speed purely by swapping the cable. Look for a pack that includes a genuinely rated cable, and if it does not, add one to your kit list before you travel.
 Long cables also cost voltage. Keep the run from pack to laptop as short as the bag allows.
 Display versus indicator lights
 Four LED dots tell you roughly a quarter of the story. A numeric display showing wattage, temperature and remaining time is worth real money on a pack you will use all day, because it is the only way to tell a slow cable from a slow pack. Several owners say the display is the feature they use most.
 Weight and multi-device behaviour
 Every 25,000mAh pack in this group lands between 400 g and 700 g. If it lives in a laptop sleeve all day, weight is the deciding spec, and the INIU at 13.8 ounces is the outlier. If it lives in a backpack or a checked bag, prioritise ports and output instead.
 For multi-device work, look for two USB-C ports that both deliver high wattage, a low-current mode for earbuds and watches, and pass-through charging if you will use the pack as a desk UPS rather than a travel spare.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best power bank for charging a laptop?
 The Anker 737 Power Bank (140W, 24,000mAh) is the best all-round choice. It matches the adapter rating of mainstream USB-C laptops, has the highest review volume of any pack in this roundup, and a smart display that shows live wattage. If you need to charge two devices at high speed, the UGREEN Nexode 25,000mAh 200W adds a second high-wattage port.
 Is it good to charge a laptop with a power bank?
 Yes, and it will not shorten battery life the way leaving a laptop on a charger constantly might. Charging a laptop from a power bank is the same USB-C Power Delivery handshake the wall adapter performs. The main caveat is thermal: a gaming laptop under sustained load will warm up when charging from a pack, and keeping it cool helps both the laptop and the pack last longer.
 How big of a power bank do I need to charge a laptop?
 For one full charge of a mainstream USB-C laptop, 20,000mAh to 25,000mAh is the practical range, which is about 74Wh to 92.5Wh at the 3.7V nominal cell voltage. Below 10,000mAh you are topping up a phone, not refilling a laptop. Above 25,000mAh you cross the 100Wh airline carry-on limit and need approval.
 How many watts should a power bank have to charge a laptop?
 Match or exceed the wattage printed on your laptop’s charger. A Chromebook needs about 30W, a thin ultrabook 45W to 65W, a mainstream USB-C laptop 100W, a 16-inch MacBook Pro or gaming laptop 140W under PD 3.1, and a workstation 200W or more. Anything lower will still charge, but slowly and often only while the laptop is idle.
 Is there a power bank that can power a laptop?
 Yes, any pack with USB-C Power Delivery at 65W or more can charge a USB-C laptop. Laptops that charge over a proprietary round barrel jack, or that need more than 200W, generally cannot be power-banked unless the manufacturer ships a USB-C adapter. A 140W PD 3.1 pack covers most ultrabooks, 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros, and most gaming laptops.
 What is the best power bank for both a laptop and a phone?
 Look for a pack with two high-wattage USB-C ports and a stated per-port breakdown, not just a total figure. The UGREEN Nexode 25,000mAh 200W gives 140W on one USB-C port and 100W on the other, so the laptop and the phone both charge quickly. Remember that total output is shared, so a phone on the wrong port can cut your laptop’s speed.
 Can you take a power bank on a plane?
 Yes, up to 100Wh in carry-on baggage only, which is roughly 27,000mAh at 3.7V. Never put a power bank in a checked bag. Packs between 101Wh and 160Wh need airline approval before you fly, and anything above 160Wh is prohibited. A swollen or damaged pack will be refused at the gate.
 Does charging a laptop with a power bank shorten its battery life?
 No more than charging from a wall adapter would. The pack negotiates the same Power Delivery profile the charger does, and the laptop manages its own battery. The two things worth avoiding are heat and sitting at 100 percent for long stretches, so keep the laptop ventilated while charging and unplug when the work is done.
 Why is my laptop charging so slowly from a power bank?
 Three usual causes. The pack’s output is below your laptop’s adapter wattage, so it charges at the pack’s limit instead. You are sharing total output across two ports, which splits the power. Or the cable is not e-marked for 5A, which throttles anything above 100W. Check the pack display first, because it shows whether the pack is delivering what it should.
 Do I need a special cable to charge a laptop from a power bank?
 Below 100W, any decent USB-C to USB-C cable works. Above 100W you need an e-marked 5A cable, and the one that ships in the box often is not. Owners in this roundup reported speeds jumping from 6-7W to 27W on the same pack purely by swapping to a certified cable. Keep the cable run short as well, since long runs add voltage drop.
 The Bottom Line on the Best Power Banks for Laptops
 The Anker 737 Power Bank (140W, 24,000mAh) remains the pick we would hand to most people in 2026. It matches the adapter rating of mainstream USB-C laptops, carries by far the deepest review history of anything in this roundup, and its smart display tells you what the pack is actually doing, which is the difference between a tool and a guessing game.
 If you charge several devices at once, the UGREEN Nexode 25,000mAh 200W gives you two high-wattage USB-C ports. If weight decides your day, the INIU at 13.8 ounces is the pick. If you need peak output for a 16-inch machine, the Anker Prime at 250W is the ceiling of this category.
 Whichever you choose, the three checks that decide the outcome are the same: match your laptop’s adapter wattage, buy a certified 5A cable if the pack is 100W or above, and keep the pack in your carry-on rather than a checked bag. Get those right and you will stop looking for outlets entirely.

 How many watts does your laptop need?
 Find the wattage printed on the charger that came with your laptop, and match or exceed it. A bank with a higher number is safe: your laptop draws what it needs, and a 100W source on a 65W laptop is not a problem.
 Thin ultrabook or Chromebook (charger 30W to 45W): minimum 30W, ideal 65W.
 13-inch and 14-inch business notebook (charger 45W to 65W): minimum 45W, ideal 65W to 100W.
 MacBook Pro 14-inch or Dell XPS class (charger 65W to 96W): minimum 65W, ideal 100W.
 MacBook Pro 16-inch or mobile workstation (charger 100W to 140W): minimum 100W, ideal 140W from a single port.
 Gaming laptop, ASUS Zephyrus or Legion class (charger 200W to 300W): minimum 100W, and carry the OEM charger as well.
 That last row is the honest one. A gaming laptop at full load can out-draw any power bank in this roundup, and users on r/ZephyrusG15 confirm these machines want 20V on USB-C fast charging. Treat a bank as an emergency top-up for those machines, not a replacement charger.
 How much capacity do you need after conversion loss?
 The printed mAh is measured at the cell voltage, not at the voltage your laptop accepts, so you never get the whole number. A 25,000mAh bank typically delivers somewhere around 14,000 to 17,500mAh of usable output once conversion loss is counted. This is the single most useful number nobody prints on the box.
 For scale, expect one full charge of a mainstream notebook plus a partial second from a 25,000mAh bank, and one full charge from a 20,000mAh unit. If you need two guaranteed full charges, buy two banks rather than one larger one, because the airline ceiling caps you anyway.
 Airline rules and the 100 Wh ceiling
 Spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on luggage and must stay under 100 watt-hours, which is roughly 27,000mAh. Anything above that needs airline approval, and no power bank of any size is permitted in checked baggage. Every bank in this roundup is rated at or under 100 Wh, with the 25,000mAh models at 91 to 92.5 Wh to leave headroom.
 Rules vary by carrier, and we would confirm the wording with your airline rather than assuming. Weight matters too, since a 621 g bank plus a laptop is real luggage, and a bag that fits the machine but not the charger is the problem this roundup is trying to solve.
 Shared wattage, cables and pass-through charging
 Two ports rated 100W each does not mean 200W to each device. Multi-port output is shared: the bank negotiates one total budget and divides it. That is why the UGREEN 130W model delivers 100W on one port and about 30W on the others, and it is the reason total-wattage figures in listings need reading carefully.
 Cables are the other half of the chain. A thin 3A cable cannot carry 140W no matter what the bank does, so look for a 5A E-marked cable or use the one included. Several banks here come with a suitable cable, which saves a trip to a cable drawer.
 Pass-through charging lets the bank charge your laptop while it refills. It is convenient, but it keeps the cells cycling and the unit warm, so treat it as a short-term bridge rather than an overnight arrangement. Anyone running a desktop-class setup for long periods should look at our portable power stations for wedding photographers , which run on AC output and are built for sustained loads rather than a laptop top-up.
 Barrel-jack laptops and the USB-C to DC route
 If your laptop charges through a round barrel connector rather than USB-C, a USB-C power bank will not work with the cable that came with it. The fix is a USB-C to DC barrel adapter matched to your machine’s voltage and polarity, and users on r/toughbook report success with a 16V supply on their setup.
 Get the voltage and polarity right, and check that the machine negotiates over the barrel connection rather than treating it as a fixed input. Some older business laptops will simply refuse, and in that case a power station with an AC outlet is the more reliable answer.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best portable power bank for laptops?
 The Anker 25,000mAh 165W Laptop Power Bank is the best all-round option in 2026. It delivers up to 100W from a single USB-C port, carries two built-in cables, refills in about two hours on a 100W charger, and sits exactly at the 100 Wh airline limit.
 How big of a power bank do I need to charge a laptop?
 A 20,000mAh to 25,000mAh bank covers a typical laptop charge once, with a partial second charge. Remember the real usable figure is lower than the printed rating because of conversion loss, so 25,000mAh behaves closer to 14,000 to 17,500mAh delivered.
 How many watts should a power bank have to charge a laptop?
 Match or exceed the wattage on your laptop charger. Thin ultrabooks need 30W to 45W, 14-inch business notebooks need 45W to 65W, and 16-inch MacBook Pro or workstation class machines need 100W to 140W. A higher-wattage bank is always safe because the laptop draws only what it needs.
 Can a 20,000mAh power bank fully charge a laptop?
 Usually yes for a thin or mid-size notebook, after accounting for conversion loss that cuts delivered capacity to roughly 60 to 70 percent of the printed rating. A 20,000mAh bank usually delivers around 12,000 to 14,000mAh, which is one full charge of most 13- and 14-inch laptops.
 Is it safe to use a power bank for a laptop?
 Yes, a USB-C Power Delivery bank is safe for a laptop because the two negotiate a voltage and current profile before charging begins, and your laptop draws only what its charger would have delivered. The two cautions are avoiding pass-through charging for long stretches and buying from a brand with real safety certification.
 Can I take a laptop power bank on a flight?
 Yes, as long as it stays under 100 watt-hours, which is about 27,000mAh, and travels in your carry-on rather than checked baggage. Spare lithium batteries are not permitted in checked luggage at all. Every power bank in this roundup is rated at or below 100 Wh, and carrier rules vary, so confirm before you travel.
 The Bottom Line on the Best Power Banks for Laptops in 2026
 After six weeks of carry, charging and weight-checking, the Anker 25,000mAh 165W Laptop Power Bank is the single best power bank for laptops most people should buy. It delivers full single-port wattage, carries its own cables, and has the largest review base here by a wide margin.
 Go with the Anker Prime at 220W if you carry a gaming machine or a 16-inch MacBook Pro, and pick the INIU 20,000mAh 65W if your laptop is thin and weight matters more than speed. Whatever you choose, match the bank to your charger wattage first, then check the airline limit before you book.

 How to Choose the Best Power Bank for Your Laptop?
 Choosing the best power banks for laptops in 2026 comes down to five variables: capacity in mAh and Wh, USB-C PD wattage, port layout, build and warranty, and whether you fly often. Below, we break down each variable with the math and the trade-offs so you can pick the right bank for your specific laptop.
 Capacity: mAh versus watt-hours explained
 Capacity in mAh (milliamp-hours) is the marketing number. Capacity in watt-hours (Wh) is the number that actually tells you how much energy is inside the bank and whether it will pass airport security. To convert mAh to Wh, multiply the mAh by the voltage (usually 3.7V for lithium-ion cells) and divide by 1000. A 20,000 mAh bank at 3.7V is about 74 Wh. A 25,000 mAh bank at 3.7V is about 92.5 Wh.
 For TSA and most international airline carry-on rules, the limit is 100 Wh per battery. Banks between 100 Wh and 160 Wh need airline approval. Anything over 160 Wh is forbidden in the cabin. That is why every laptop-class bank on this list sits at 20,000-25,000 mAh — it is the sweet spot where you maximize capacity while staying safely under 100 Wh.
 One more wrinkle: a 25,000 mAh bank will not deliver 25,000 mAh of charge to your laptop. Voltage conversion from the bank’s 3.7V cells to your laptop’s 20V USB-C PD input loses 30-40 percent of the energy as heat. In our real-world testing, a 25K bank that advertises 92.5 Wh of stored energy delivered roughly 60-65 Wh to a MacBook Pro 14 — about 70 percent efficiency. That is normal and expected, but it explains why your laptop only refills once even on a “25,000 mAh” bank.
 USB-C Power Delivery: the wattage you actually need
 Wattage is the single most important spec for laptop charging. A bank with 100W output will fast-charge a 100W laptop. A bank with 45W will charge a MacBook Air at full speed but will throttle a 16-inch MacBook Pro. Here is a rough tiering:
 30W — Phones, tablets, Nintendo Switch, very light laptops. Not enough for most MacBooks.
 45W — MacBook Air, Chromebook, iPad Pro fast charging. Slow for bigger laptops.
 65W — Minimum threshold for fast-charging most 13-14 inch laptops including Dell XPS 13, ThinkPad X1 Carbon, and MacBook Pro 13.
 100W — The sweet spot for 14-16 inch laptops. Handles MacBook Pro 14 and most Dell XPS 15 use cases.
 140W — Required for MacBook Pro 16 under full load, Framework 16, Razer Blade, MSI gaming laptops.
 240W+ — Reserved for 240W USB PD 3.1 EPR laptops and multi-laptop setups (Anker Prime 300W, EcoFlow Rapid Pro X).
 If your laptop came with a 65W or 100W USB-C charger, match the bank to that wattage. Do not pay extra for a 140W bank you do not need.
 Ports, cables, and pass-through charging
 Most modern power banks ship with two to four ports: a mix of USB-C and USB-A. Look for at least two USB-C ports if you regularly charge a laptop plus a phone. Built-in cables are a strong convenience feature — they eliminate the forgotten-cable problem that has killed more trips than dead batteries. Anker’s 20K Travel Essential and 25K 165W both ship with integrated USB-C cables rated for 10,000+ bend cycles.
 Pass-through charging means using the bank to charge your laptop while the bank itself is plugged into a wall outlet. It is convenient but slower — most banks throttle output to preserve battery health. A few banks (UGREEN Nexode 25K included) have firmware quirks that cause pass-through to cycle on and off. If you rely on a desk setup with a bank chained through a dock, test your specific configuration before relying on it.
 TSA, airline rules, and the 100Wh limit
 US TSA and most international carriers (IATA) allow lithium-ion power banks in carry-on luggage up to 100 Wh without airline approval. Between 100 Wh and 160 Wh requires airline approval, usually granted but not guaranteed. Above 160 Wh is forbidden. Banks must be carried on, never checked. After several in-flight battery fire incidents in recent years, some airlines have tightened rules and added lithium battery tracking forms — check your carrier’s policy before flying.
 Every laptop-class bank on this list sits under 100 Wh and is safe for cabin luggage. The 25K class banks (Anker, UGREEN, INIU) are around 90-92 Wh, leaving a small safety margin for label rounding.
 Voltage conversion, efficiency, and the 70 percent rule
 Your laptop power bank stores energy at 3.7V (the natural voltage of lithium-ion cells). Your laptop charges at 20V (or 28V for USB PD 3.1 EPR). Converting between the two wastes energy as heat. Real-world efficiency is 60-70 percent. That is why a 25,000 mAh / 92.5 Wh bank only delivers about 60-65 Wh to your laptop.
 This explains the most common complaint on r/UsbCHardware and r/laptops: “Why does my 25,000 mAh bank only refill my laptop once?” It is doing exactly what it should. The mAh number is real but it is mAh at 3.7V, not at 20V.
 Brand reliability and warranty comparison
 Anker, UGREEN, and INIU are the three brands we trust most in this category. Anker’s 18-month warranty is the industry baseline. UGREEN matches that on most models. INIU ships 3-year warranties across its lineup. NOBIS offers a 3-year warranty on its 20K 45W. Lion Energy goes further with a 5-year warranty on its premium models — but those are not on this list.
 For Smashing Robotics readers, brand reliability matters because the same bank often powers a laptop and a robot controller. We have seen cheap Amazon banks fail in under a year, with capacity fade and port corrosion. Stick to the established brands.
 Robotics, drone, and field charging use case
 For our regular Smashing Robotics audience, laptop power banks double as field power supplies. The 100W USB-C PD output on the Anker 25K, UGREEN Nexode, and INIU 25K models is enough to run an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano dev kit, charge a DJI Mavic 3 battery bank, or top up a ROS-powered mobile robot’s 19V logic supply via a USB-C PD trigger cable. For multi-day field robotics work, we recommend pairing a 25K bank with a USB-C PD buck converter to step down to 12V or 19V for legacy robot hardware. If you are wiring a robot power system safely, our guide on how to wire a robot power system safely covers the fusing and grounding rules.
 For powering individual components, a USB-C PD trigger cable can negotiate 12V or 19V directly from any 100W laptop power bank — useful for robot sub-systems like motor controllers, depth cameras, and LIDAR units. See our guide on powering a robot from a wall adapter safely for the broader setup, and our piece on why robots use separate power for logic and motors for why you want isolated supplies on a robot platform. If you are building a tethered mobile robot, Power over Ethernet is another option worth understanding for low-power auxiliary hardware like vision stacks and depth cameras.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Which power bank is good for laptops?
 The best power banks for laptops in 2026 are 20,000-25,000 mAh models with at least 65W USB-C PD output. The Anker Laptop Power Bank 25K 165W is our top pick for most users, the UGREEN Nexode 25K 145W is the premium pick for 140W laptops, and the INIU 25K 100W is the best value. All three stay under the 100Wh TSA carry-on limit.
 How many mAh to charge a laptop?
 For a full laptop recharge, aim for at least 20,000 mAh (about 74 Wh). For a 25,000 mAh / 92 Wh bank, expect roughly one full MacBook Pro 14 refill, accounting for 30-40 percent voltage conversion loss. A 10,000 mAh bank will only top up a MacBook Air by 30-40 percent.
 Will a 100W charger damage a 65W laptop?
 No. USB-C Power Delivery is a negotiated protocol. Your laptop will only draw the wattage it is designed for, even if the charger or power bank can supply more. A 100W bank safely charges a 65W laptop at full 65W speed. There is no over-charge risk because the laptop controls the draw.
 How do I travel with a portable charger on a plane?
 Power banks must go in carry-on luggage, never checked. Under US TSA and IATA rules, lithium-ion power banks up to 100 Wh are allowed without airline approval. Banks between 100 Wh and 160 Wh require airline approval. Above 160 Wh is forbidden. Every laptop power bank on this list is under 100 Wh for safe cabin travel.
 How do you fast charge a power bank itself?
 To fast-charge a power bank, you need a USB-C PD wall charger that matches or exceeds the bank’s input wattage. The Anker 25K 165W refills in about 1.5-2 hours with a 100W PD input. The UGREEN Nexode 25K refills in 2 hours with a 65W input. Using a 20W phone charger will stretch the same refill to 5-6 hours.
 Is there a power bank that can power a gaming laptop?
 Yes, but you need one with 140W or higher USB-C PD 3.1 output. The UGREEN Nexode 25K 145W delivers a stable 118-132W to a 16-inch MacBook Pro under load. The Anker Prime 300W and HyperJuice 245W handle the heaviest gaming laptops at 240W+. Budget 45W banks will not keep up with a gaming laptop under full load.
 Final Verdict
 The best power banks for laptops in 2026 all share three traits: at least 20,000 mAh of capacity, at least 65W USB-C PD output, and a weight under about 500 g. Within that envelope, the right pick depends on your use case.
 For most people, the Anker Laptop Power Bank 25K 165W is the right answer. It charges three devices at once, has built-in cables, and sits under the TSA limit. For power users running MacBook Pro 16 or gaming laptops, the UGREEN Nexode 25K 145W is worth the premium. For buyers on a budget, the INIU 25K 100W delivers 90 percent of the performance at a much lower price, backed by a 3-year warranty.
 Whichever bank you choose, remember the 70 percent rule: a 25,000 mAh bank will deliver roughly 60-65 Wh to your laptop after voltage conversion losses. That is normal, expected, and the reason real-world charging numbers always look lower than the marketing capacity. For field robotics, drone ground stations, and travel workflows, the same banks power your laptop and your robot hardware — a 100W USB-C PD trigger cable turns any of these banks into a 12V or 19V supply for legacy controllers.

 Pros: True 140W single-port charging matches the laptop’s own charger; 250W total across three ports runs a laptop, phone, and tablet at once; LCD shows live wattage and time-to-full; 99.56Wh keeps it flyable.
 Cons: The priciest pick here; a genuinely heavy metal brick; no built-in cable. Worth skipping if you mostly charge phones, want something pocketable, or do not need three-device full-wattage output — you would be paying for headroom you will never use.
 See price at Amazon → 
 Best for travel: Anker Laptop Power Bank (25K, 165W)
 Anker Laptop Power Bank (165W). Image: Anker. 
 This is the one to pack for a flight. The cables are built in: one retractable USB-C, one fixed USB-C that doubles as a carrying strap, plus two more ports — four devices at once, up to 165W total, with each USB-C port rated at 100W and a 33W USB-A alongside. No tangle of loose cables to fish out at a cramped gate, which matters more than it sounds. Across verified owner reports, reviewers describe charging a MacBook Air from 20% to 90% in about an hour with capacity still left over for phones. A front display shows percentage, live in/out wattage, and recharge time.
 Pros: Built-in retractable and strap cables mean nothing loose to pack; four devices at once up to 165W total; front display shows live in/out wattage; recharges a MacBook Air 20–90% in about an hour with reserve to spare.
 Cons: Each port tops out at 100W, not 140W, so a power-hungry 16-inch laptop will not hit its absolute fastest; it is also chunky. Worth skipping if you specifically need 140W single-port speed for a large MacBook Pro or a gaming laptop — step up to the Prime or the UGREEN below.
 See price at Amazon → 
 Best value: UGREEN Nexode 25,000mAh (145W)
 UGREEN Nexode (145W). Image: UGREEN. 
 The UGREEN Nexode delivers the headline number that matters — a 140W single USB-C port — for noticeably less than the Anker Prime. Across expert reviews, it consistently scores as delivering roughly 90% of the Prime’s real-world capability at a significantly lower price. Its second USB-C port runs at 65W and the USB-A handles 22.5W, so charging three devices at once is comfortable. At around 496 grams it is reasonable for the capacity. UGREEN quotes enough capacity to recharge an iPhone over five times or nearly fully refill a 14-inch MacBook Pro. It is true full-speed laptop charging without paying the flagship premium.
 Pros: Full 140W single-port charging for much less than the Prime; roughly 90% of the Prime’s real-world capability; comfortable three-device charging (65W second USB-C, 22.5W USB-A); reasonable ~496g for the capacity.
 Cons: Total combined output is lower than the Prime’s 250W, so it cannot fast-charge multiple power-hungry devices at once; no built-in cable. Worth skipping if you are a road warrior who routinely charges two laptops, or a laptop and tablet at full tilt at once — the Prime’s extra headroom is worth it for you.
 See price at Amazon → 
 Slimmest for a laptop bag: Baseus Blade 100W (20,000mAh)
 Baseus Blade (100W). Image: Baseus. 
 Every other pick here is a thick brick. The Baseus Blade is the flat one — a wide, thin slab that slides into a laptop sleeve or a bag’s back pocket instead of consuming a fist-sized chunk of space. It outputs 100W from USB-C, runs two USB-C and two USB-A ports for four devices total, and includes a display showing live charging stats. For an ultrabook, a Steam Deck, or an iPad, 100W is genuinely sufficient, and the form factor is the entire point.
 Pros: Flat, thin profile slides into a sleeve or back pocket; four devices total across two USB-C and two USB-A ports; display shows live charging stats; 100W is plenty for an ultrabook, Steam Deck, or iPad.
 Cons: 100W is the entry point to laptop-class charging, not the ceiling — a 16-inch MacBook Pro or a gaming laptop will not charge at full speed; 20,000mAh is less reserve than the 25K picks. Worth skipping if you drive a large, high-draw laptop or want maximum hours per charge — one of the 25,000mAh, 140W options is the better call.
 See price at Amazon → 
 Also considered
 A few others surfaced repeatedly and deserve a mention. Anker also makes a Prime 26,250mAh (300W) with even more combined headroom — two USB-C ports, a 140W single-port max, 300W total — for users who want to push the ceiling further. UGREEN’s Nexode 25,000mAh (200W) sits between the value pick and the flagships on total output. Both are strong options; for most people the four picks above strike the better balance of wattage, capacity, and price.
 How to choose in one minute
 Match the wattage to your laptop, not the capacity to your anxiety. Running a 16-inch MacBook Pro or a gaming laptop? Insist on a 140W single-port bank — the Prime or the UGREEN 145W. Carrying an ultrabook, a MacBook Air, a Steam Deck, or an iPad? 100W is genuinely enough and buys you a slimmer, lighter pack. Want the fewest cables to manage? The Anker Laptop bank with built-in cables is the answer. And whatever you choose, stay under 100Wh if you ever fly.
 Frequently asked questions
 Can I bring these on a plane? Yes — every pick here falls under the 100Wh limit airlines set for spare lithium batteries, so they are allowed in carry-on bags (never checked). A 30,000mAh-class pack exceeds that ceiling and requires airline approval.
 Will a 140W bank charge my laptop while I use it? For most laptops, yes. The whole point of this class is that output meets or exceeds what your laptop draws under load, so the battery holds or climbs rather than slowly dropping. Very high-draw gaming laptops are the exception and may still lose ground during heavy sessions.
 Do I need 250W or 300W? Only if you are fast-charging several power-hungry devices at the same time. A single laptop never needs more than its own charger’s rated wattage — typically 100W or 140W. Those higher combined-output figures are about feeding multiple devices at once, not charging one device faster.
 Is more mAh always better? No. Past roughly 25,000mAh you run into the 100Wh airline limit, and the pack gets heavier for diminishing real-world gain. For most people a 25,000mAh, 140W bank is the sweet spot: flyable, fast, and not absurdly heavy.
 Why does my old power bank drain while my laptop is plugged in? Because it cannot output enough watts. An 18W–30W phone bank simply cannot keep pace with a laptop’s draw, so you are charging slower than you are consuming. That is exactly the problem this entire category solves.

 Best high-performance alternative: Anker Prime, but check the exact model

 Best high-output competitor: UGREEN Nexode Pro 25,000mAh 200W

Those specifications make it a legitimate alternative to the Anker A1695 for users who prefer UGREEN’s port arrangement or find a better price.
 The same caution applies: 200W is a combined figure, not a promise that one laptop will receive 200W. The two 100W USB-C limits, the bank’s power-sharing rules, the cable, and the laptop’s own charging limit determine the actual result. The available review information does not provide enough of its specifications here to make a responsible performance comparison, so treat it as a model worth investigating rather than a replacement for the better-documented picks above.  How to choose the right power bank
 1. Compare watt-hours, not just milliamp-hours
 Milliamp-hours describe the charge stored by the internal battery cells. They do not equal the amount delivered to a phone or laptop because a power bank must convert its cell voltage to the device’s charging voltage, and that process loses energy.
 A rough conversion is:
 Watt-hours ≈ milliamp-hours × nominal cell voltage ÷ 1,000 
 The cell voltage and the manufacturer’s rated energy matter. Anker lists the A1695 at 90Wh and says its 25,000mAh bank may deliver approximately 13,750mAh to 17,500mAh to devices after a stated 30–45% reduction from conversion and circuitry losses. The actual result varies with the phone or laptop battery, charging efficiency, temperature, cable, simultaneous use, and whether the device is being used while charging.
 As practical sizing bands:
 5,000–10,000mAh: portable, phone-focused, and suitable for emergency top-ups.
 20,000–27,000mAh: more suitable for tablets, handheld consoles, cameras, and occasional laptop charging.
 Above that range: useful for high-endurance or high-output work, but increasingly heavy and more complicated for air travel.
 These are selection guidelines, not promises of a specific number of full charges. A 20,000mAh bank does not automatically charge every phone four times.

 2. Check USB-C Power Delivery and per-port output
 A large capacity label cannot make a bank suitable for a laptop. Look for USB-C Power Delivery output, the maximum output from each port, combined-output behavior, and the maximum input used to recharge the bank.
 USB Power Delivery 3.1 expands USB-C charging capability to 240W, but that higher rate only matters when the power bank, laptop, charger, and cable support compatible power profiles. A bank advertised as 165W or 200W may provide only 100W to one laptop, or less when other devices are connected.
 Cable capability matters too. A cable that came with a phone may not support the power level advertised by a high-output bank. For high-wattage laptop charging, use a USB-C cable explicitly rated for the required wattage and confirm that it supports the relevant USB PD specification.
 3. Understand simultaneous charging and recharge time
 Manufacturers commonly quote the best total output with a particular number of connected devices. Connecting a third or fourth device can change the power distribution and slow laptop charging. If you regularly charge a laptop and phone together, look for a published multi-port output table rather than relying on the largest number on the front of the box.
 Recharge speed is a separate specification. UGREEN lists up to 100W input for the Nexode Pro, while the cited product information does not establish one universal recharge figure for every Anker Prime model or the A1695. A large bank with a slow input can take much of a day to refill, especially with a low-wattage wall charger.
 4. Treat Qi2 as a convenience feature
 Qi2 and MagSafe-style magnetic charging solve an alignment problem and make short phone top-ups convenient. They also add conversion and transmission losses and are generally slower than a direct USB-C connection. Magnetic charging is worth paying for if you want an attached kickstand, cable-free use, or easier alignment; it is not the best reason to choose a bank for a laptop, tablet, or long off-grid trip.
 5. Check the watt-hour rating before flying
 The FAA requires spare lithium-ion batteries, including power banks, to be carried in carry-on baggage rather than checked baggage. Batteries rated from 0 to 100Wh are generally allowed for passenger travel. Batteries from 101Wh to 160Wh generally require airline approval, and batteries above 160Wh are not permitted on passenger aircraft. Airlines may impose stricter limits, including limits on the number of spare batteries.
 Use the printed or manufacturer-listed Wh rating when checking travel suitability. Do not calculate from a marketing mAh figure unless you know the battery’s nominal voltage. The Anker A1695’s listed 90Wh rating is below the general 100Wh threshold, but its size is close enough that checking the label and airline policy is sensible. Keep it accessible in your carry-on and protect the ports from short circuits.

 6. Evaluate safety without trusting blanket claims
 No product should be described as incapable of overheating or universally safe. Instead, check the manufacturer’s documented protection features, warranty terms, recall notices, support reputation, and the condition of the specific unit. Do not use a bank or cable that is swollen, cracked, unusually hot, wet, or physically damaged. Avoid leaving a charging bank in a hot vehicle or under bedding where heat cannot escape.
 Review methodology is also part of trust. WIRED says it tests each incoming portable charger for at least two weeks, checks charging performance across several devices, and considers usability, warranties, customer service, user reviews, and longer-term reliability for some top picks. Expert Reviews describes measuring USB-A and USB-C output with a USB power meter, testing wireless charging, measuring recharge rate from a 65W charger, and running a 15-minute smartphone charging test.
 The Guardian describes using a custom fan-based dummy-load setup to measure input, output, charging speed, and efficiency, followed by real-world charging tests with an iPhone 17 Pro and Galaxy S26 Ultra.  Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best power bank for most people in 2026?
 The Anker Laptop Power Bank 25K 165W (A1695) is the best general-purpose choice for most people who need to charge phones, tablets, handheld consoles, and USB-C laptops. It offers 100W from one USB-C connection and 165W combined under its specified two-device configuration, but it weighs about 21oz and is overkill for phone-only use.
 How many watt-hours can a power bank have on a plane?
 The FAA generally allows spare lithium-ion batteries from 0 to 100Wh in carry-on baggage. Batteries from 101 to 160Wh generally require airline approval, and those above 160Wh are not allowed on passenger aircraft. Power banks must not be packed in checked baggage, and individual airlines can be stricter.
 Is Qi2 wireless charging better than USB-C?
 Qi2 is more convenient because magnetic alignment makes it easy to attach a phone and use a kickstand. USB-C is normally faster and more efficient, so it is the better choice when you need maximum battery delivered or want to charge a tablet or laptop.
 The Bottom Line
 Bottom line: Buy the Anker A1695 if you want one capable bank for several devices and can accept its weight. Choose the MagGo 10K for magnetic phone charging, the Nimble Champ Pro or Cuktech 10 Mini for a small everyday backup, the Goal Zero Flip 24 for a day hike, and the BioLite Charge 80 PD for longer outdoor trips.
